questions.title: Why did the Eighth Circuit vacate and remand the MFLSA claim instead of just deciding whether Cohen could recover penalties?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture of the MFLSA part of this case. Cohen stipulated that he had already been paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages he claimed were owed, and the only thing left seems to be statutory penalties that would be paid to the Commissioner rather than to him personally. The court then says it has a “serious concern” about jurisdiction and remands for the district court to determine whether the claim is moot. Why couldn't the court of appeals just decide the statutory-penalty issue directly? Is the idea that Article III jurisdiction has to be resolved first before the court can reach the merits, and the record was insufficient to decide whether the challenged overtime policy was still in place?

questions.title: How can a plaintiff have standing to seek civil penalties that are payable only to the government?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw for the proposition that civil penalties can sometimes redress a plaintiff's injury by deterring future violations, even when the money doesn't go to the plaintiff. But here the court also notes that the penalties under the MFLSA would go to the Commissioner, not to Cohen. I'm having trouble understanding the redressability analysis. What exactly must a plaintiff show to have standing for this kind of penalty claim, and why might that be harder here than in Laidlaw? Is Judge Kobes's concurrence suggesting that deterrence-based standing may not carry over automatically from environmental cases to wage-and-hour statutes?

questions.title: Why did the court read Minnesota's Payment of Wages Act as allowing only the Commissioner—not employees—to recover the average daily wage penalty?
questions.question_body: On the MPWA claim, Cohen argued that the text of Minn. Stat. § 181.101 authorized him to recover average daily wage penalties, but the court said only the Commissioner may seek those penalties. I'm struggling with the statutory interpretation. Section 181.171 says an employee can sue for violations of certain wage statutes and recover “civil penalties or damages provided for in the section violated.” If that's true, why doesn't that incorporate the penalty language from § 181.101 into a private action? Is the court basically saying that because § 181.101 specifically describes the Commissioner serving a demand and then collecting the penalty, that specific enforcement mechanism overrides the more general private right language in § 181.171?

questions.title: What role did the comparison to Minnesota statutes §§ 181.13 and 181.14 play in the court's interpretation of § 181.101?
questions.question_body: The opinion emphasizes that the Minnesota legislature ‘knew how’ to expressly give employees the right to collect penalties in other wage statutes, like §§ 181.13 and 181.14, but did not do so in § 181.101. I'm not sure how strong that inference is supposed to be. Is this an application of expressio unius or some other canon? Also, how much weight do courts usually give to comparisons across related statutes when the statute at issue already has a private right of action elsewhere in the same chapter?

questions.title: Why was Cohen's Minnesota Wage Theft Act claim treated as waived or inadequately briefed on appeal?
questions.question_body: For the MWTA claim, the court says Cohen complained that the district court gave little discussion to the issue, but then the Eighth Circuit refuses to disturb the dismissal because he pointed to no statutory authority allowing civil penalties and made no meaningful argument for reversal. I'm confused about the appellate practice point here. If a party thinks the district court overlooked a claim, what exactly does the party need to do on appeal to preserve it? Was the problem that Cohen failed to identify an actual remedy under § 181.032, or that he failed to develop the argument enough in his briefing, or both?

questions.title: Why did the court refuse to consider Cohen's request for an injunction ordering Consilio to rescind its overtime policy?
questions.question_body: The court says Cohen originally requested certain forms of injunctive relief in the complaint but later asked for different relief in summary judgment briefing—namely, an order requiring Consilio to withdraw the 2019 overtime policy. The court then says the issue was not properly before it because new claims must be raised through an amended complaint, not in opposition briefs. I'm trying to understand the line between a new claim and a new remedy. If the underlying theory is still that the policy violates Minnesota wage law, why isn't this just a different form of equitable relief rather than a new claim? Or is the court saying that the requested injunction was materially different enough from the pleaded relief that Rule 15 required amendment?

questions.title: What effect did the parties' stipulations have on the scope of the case and the court's analysis?
questions.question_body: The parties stipulated that Cohen had been paid all overtime wages and all MFLSA liquidated damages he alleged he was owed, and they also agreed that resolving Consilio's summary judgment motion first could fully resolve the case if Consilio won. I'm not sure how much those stipulations legally narrowed the dispute. Did they effectively eliminate any live controversy as to damages, leaving only penalties and equitable relief? And if so, why didn't that automatically moot the whole case? I'm especially confused about how stipulations interact with mootness when the plaintiff still argues there is an ongoing unlawful policy that should be deterred or enjoined.
